questions.q: A scenario clearly needs a SQL-first, T-SQL-queryable store, but one option says 'Lakehouse' instead of 'Warehouse.' What trap does this illustrate?
options: Similar-sounding item types being swapped for their lookalike
An absolute-wording trap
A buried qualifier at the end of the stem
An over-broad security control
questions.explain: Trap 1 is exactly this: Lakehouse and Warehouse sound similar and get swapped in wrong options — re-read the noun, not just the concept.

questions.q: Two options both solve a scenario, but one stays entirely inside native Fabric features and the other bolts on an external Azure service. Which is usually correct on DP-700?
options: The native Fabric option — the exam tests Fabric, not everything Azure could theoretically do
The external Azure option, because it's always more powerful
Neither — DP-700 never tests feature selection
Both are equally likely to be correct
questions.explain: Trap 2: when a native Fabric feature already solves the problem, an external bolt-on is the overcomplicated wrong answer.

questions.q: Why should options containing words like 'always,' 'never,' or 'must' get extra scrutiny?
options: Absolute wording is frequently false, since real systems have exceptions — though it isn't automatically wrong
Because those words are always wrong with no exceptions
Because those words only appear in correct answers
Because DP-700 never uses absolute language
questions.explain: Trap 3 isn't a blind rule — it's a signal to slow down and check whether an absolute claim is quietly overreaching.

questions.q: A question stem describes a normal scenario for three sentences, then adds 'but the team has no Spark experience' at the very end. What does this illustrate?
options: A buried qualifier that can flip which answer is correct
An example of an over-broad security control
A lookalike item-type trap
Proof that the stem should be skimmed, not read fully
questions.explain: Trap 4: the qualifier at the end of a stem is often load-bearing — read the whole stem before evaluating options.

questions.q: What is the single most common trap pattern across Lessons 35 and 36's practice sets?
options: Picking a real but broader-than-needed control instead of the narrowest one that satisfies the scenario
Confusing KQL syntax with T-SQL syntax
Forgetting that Fabric requires a paid Azure subscription
Assuming Fabric has no security features at all
questions.explain: Trap 5 generalizes the security and monitoring practice sets: DP-700 rewards the narrowest correct answer, not the broadest one that would technically also work.

questions.q: What do all five traps in this lesson have in common?
options: The wrong option is a real feature that's correct in some other scenario, just not this one
The wrong option is always a fabricated feature that doesn't exist
The wrong option is always the first one listed
The wrong option always involves KQL
questions.explain: The shared shape across all five traps: real feature, right somewhere else, wrong for this specific scenario's constraints.
